title: What Human Rights Are
hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.
key_points: Human rights are rights held by every person simply by virtue of being human.
They are universal (for everyone), inalienable (cannot be justly taken away), and indivisible.
They span civil-political rights (speech, fair trial) and social-economic rights (education, health).
They set a standard above any single government — a claim states should respect, not grant.
content_html: Human rights rest on a deceptively simple but historically radical idea: that there are certain rights every person holds simply by virtue of being human — not because a king granted them, a constitution lists them, or a government of the day approves. On this view, a person in any country, of any status, holds these rights, and a government's job is to respect and protect them rather than to bestow or withhold them. That is what makes human rights a claim that stands above any particular state.
extra_html: Several features define them. They are universal — held by everyone, everywhere, regardless of nationality, sex, religion, or other status. They are inalienable — they cannot justly be taken away or signed away, even if a government tries. And they are usually described as indivisible and interdependent: you cannot cleanly rank or remove one without undermining the others. Their content is broad. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the common division into civil and political rights — such as freedom of speech, freedom from torture, and the right to a fair trial, which mainly demand that the state not do certain things — and economic, social, and cultural rights — such as education, health, and an adequate standard of living, which call for positive provision. The relationship between these and the older idea of civil liberties is close: civil liberties are typically the protections a particular state guarantees its own people, while human rights are framed as belonging to all people and binding on all states. The power of the concept is precisely its universality — and the central difficulty, taken up by the institutions built to defend it, is how to make a right that everyone holds actually enforceable against a government that violates it.

related.title: Civil Liberties vs Civil Rights
related.hook: Two terms people mix up: liberties are freedoms from government interference; rights are protections to be treated equally.

related.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
related.hook: After a world war and the Holocaust, nations did something unprecedented: they wrote down, together, a common list of rights belonging to everyone on Earth.

related.title: Equality & Minority Rights
related.hook: Majority rule can become majority tyranny. Equality before the law and minority rights are how democracies stop the many from trampling the few.

related.title: Three Generations of Rights
related.hook: Human rights didn't all arrive at once. A useful map sorts them into three 'generations,' each born of a different era's struggles and demanding something different of the state.

related.title: Refugees & Asylum
related.hook: When your own government becomes the threat, your last protection is the right to flee and seek safety elsewhere — the principle at the heart of refugee law.

flashcards.prompt: What makes human rights distinctive as a kind of right?
flashcards.back_html: They belong to every person simply by being human — universal and inalienable, not granted by, or dependent on, any particular government.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean that human rights are 'inalienable'?

choices.text: They cannot be justly taken away or surrendered
They expire after a fixed number of years
They apply only to citizens of one country

flashcards.explanation_html: Inalienable means the rights cannot legitimately be stripped away — they are held permanently by virtue of being a person.

flashcards.prompt: Which pairing reflects the broad scope of human rights?

choices.text: Civil-political rights (speech, fair trial) and social-economic rights (education, health)
Only the right to own property
Only the rights of government officials

flashcards.explanation_html: Human rights span both freedoms from state interference and claims to basic well-being like education and health.
